fields.before: Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) is a flood of inflammatory signals released when immune cells are activated en masse, producing fever, low blood pressure and sometimes organ failure. It occurs with CAR-T cell therapy, T-cell engagers and some other bispecifics, is graded by ASTCT criteria and is managed with tocilizumab, which blocks the IL-6 receptor, and steroids. Step-up dosing and prophylactic tocilizumab reduce its incidence, and outpatient administration of bispecifics is now possible. The term is referenced by the Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, Multiple myeloma and Small-cell lung cancer entries, by the drug records for Tisagenlecleucel, Lisocabtagene maraleucel, Epcoritamab, Xaluritamig and Pasritamig, and by the ELIANA trial.
fields.after:
Cytokine release syndrome can follow activation by engineered immune cells or T-cell-engaging treatments. Signals from several cell types can contribute to fever, hypotension, hypoxia and other organ effects. Infection or other conditions can produce similar findings or coexist with the syndrome.

The 2019 ASTCT consensus defines and grades CRS using attributed clinical findings, including fever at onset and the blood-pressure or oxygen support required. Its scale is a reporting framework, not a management algorithm. The 2026 ASTCT consensus expands the toxicity framework, but its detailed criteria were not accessible for this entry; the numerical grading below is explicitly the 2019 version. Product, disease, preparation, observation window and treated denominator must accompany any incidence estimate.

before: Lymphoma: Lymphoma Action says almost everyone treated with engineered T-cell therapy has some level of cytokine release syndrome, that it most commonly develops within 10 days of the infusion, and that most cases are mild and easily treated. The signs it lists are fever and chills, a rapid heart rate, low blood pressure, low oxygen, headache, and feeling or being sick. Severe cases are treated with oxygen, fluids, steroids and tocilizumab, and usually improve within a few days. Around one person in five who has this treatment needs intensive care.
after: How CRS is graded, from the ASTCT 2019 consensus. The definition requires a fever of 38 degrees Celsius or higher that cannot be attributed to another cause. Severity is then the more severe of two findings, again not attributable to another cause. Grade 1 has neither. Grade 2 is low blood pressure that does not need vasopressors and/or oxygen by low-flow nasal cannula (up to 6 litres a minute) or blow-by. Grade 3 is one vasopressor, with or without vasopressin, and/or high-flow cannula, face mask, non-rebreather mask or Venturi mask. Grade 4 is multiple vasopressors, excluding vasopressin, and/or positive pressure such as CPAP, BiPAP or intubation. Once someone has had a fever-lowering or anti-cytokine treatment such as tocilizumab or steroids, fever is no longer needed to grade later severity: the grade then follows blood pressure and oxygen, and the person still counts as having CRS until the signs resolve. Organ toxicities linked to CRS are graded separately and do not change the CRS grade, and neurotoxicity during or after CRS is scored on the neurotoxicity scale, not added here. The 2026 ASTCT update (Perales et al.) convened experts to consider updating CRS, ICANS and haemophagocytic-lymphohistiocytosis-like grading, but only its abstract could be read, so whether it keeps, changes or relaxes any of these 2019 rules is not stated here; a report should say which version graded it.

Reading CRS without over-reading a cytokine level. CRS is a clinical syndrome, graded from attributed findings and not from a cytokine concentration. In a mouse model of CD19 CAR T-cell CRS, severity was mediated not by CAR T-cell-derived cytokines but by IL-6, IL-1 and nitric oxide from the recipient's macrophages, and IL-1 blockade abated it (Giavridis et al.); that supports a multicell amplification mechanism and does not show the same sources or shares in every human product. Infection and other conditions can cause or accompany the same findings, so the cause of a fever cannot be read from timing alone. A comparable report gives its grading version, observation window and treated denominator, with onset, maximum grade, interventions and resolution. Safety belongs to the product, disease, tumour burden and preparation, so experience with one blood-cancer product does not supply a solid-tumour product's rate, and no severe CRS in a small early study does not rule out uncommon events. CRS is a different problem from injury to healthy tissue that carries the target (on-target, off-tumour) and from neurotoxicity (ICANS). The treatment need not carry a cytokine payload to trigger endogenous inflammatory signalling. Tumour response does not establish acceptable inflammatory risk, and mild CRS does not establish lack of anticancer activity. Stopping a treatment input does not guarantee immediate removal of released signals or established injury. In a fictional early study, no severe CRS and a modest cytokine rise would not make every fever harmless CRS: attribution, clinical findings, a named grading framework, treated denominator and observation window are still needed.

fields.before: ICANS, the immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, is the confusion, speech difficulty and occasionally seizures that can follow CAR-T cell therapy or bispecific T-cell engagers. It is more common with CD28-costimulated CAR-T products and is managed with steroids, and a delayed parkinsonism has been seen rarely with BCMA-directed CAR-T such as cilta-cel. The term appears in the Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Multiple myeloma entries and in the drug records for Tisagenlecleucel, Obecabtagene autoleucel, Lisocabtagene maraleucel, Idecabtagene vicleucel and Epcoritamab. It also features in the bottlenecks on toxicity and the limits of the patient, on manufacturing living medicines, and on toxicity and quality of life being undervalued.
fields.after:
Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, or ICANS, is a neurologic syndrome associated with immune-effector-cell therapy. Changes in language, attention, handwriting or awareness and more severe findings such as seizures need assessment against baseline and alternative explanations. An immune-marker plot does not establish the syndrome.

The 2019 ASTCT adult framework combines the immune effector cell-associated encephalopathy (ICE) score with consciousness, seizures, motor findings and raised intracranial pressure or cerebral oedema. Children require age-appropriate assessment. The 2026 consensus also addresses non-ICANS neurologic toxicities; its detailed tables were not accessible for this entry. Neurologic events and recovery need their own record rather than being inferred from resolution of CRS.

before: Lymphoma: Lymphoma Action says around one person in four treated with engineered T-cell therapy develops neurotoxicity, that it generally appears within 28 days of the infusion and often within a few days, and that symptoms are usually mild and resolve in a week or two. The signs it lists are confusion, speech problems, difficulty writing, headache and dizziness, shaking or tremor, and difficulty moving. Seizures and brain swelling are the serious forms. Someone who develops it is advised not to drive for 8 weeks from the onset of symptoms, and the requirement to have another adult present for the four weeks after infusion exists because the person affected is often the last to notice.
after: How ICANS is graded, from the ASTCT 2019 consensus. For adults, the grade is the most severe of five findings, none attributable to another cause. The 10-point ICE screen of orientation, naming, command-following, writing and attention scores 7 to 9 for grade 1, 3 to 6 for grade 2, 0 to 2 for grade 3, and 0 because the person is unarousable and cannot be tested for grade 4; an ICE of 0 in someone who is awake with global aphasia can still be grade 3. Level of consciousness counts only if no other cause such as a sedating medicine explains it: awakens spontaneously, awakens to voice, only to touch, or unarousable or requiring vigorous or repeated tactile stimulation. Any seizure that resolves rapidly, or EEG-only seizures that resolve with treatment, is grade 3, and prolonged (over 5 minutes) or repeated seizures without return to baseline are grade 4. Deep focal motor weakness is grade 4, while tremor and myoclonus may be graded on CTCAE but do not change the ICANS grade. Focal oedema on imaging is grade 3; diffuse oedema, posturing, cranial nerve VI palsy, papilloedema or Cushing's triad is grade 4; intracranial haemorrhage is excluded from ICANS grading. So ICE is a screen for encephalopathy and one input, not the whole examination: a person with an ICE of 3 who has a generalised seizure is grade 3, and headache alone is not a useful marker. The 2026 ASTCT consensus abstract adds categories such as non-ICANS neurological toxicities (parkinsonism, cranial nerve palsies, polyneuropathies) and tumour inflammation-associated neurotoxicity; their criteria, and any change to how ICE is used, were not readable here.

What is known about mechanism, timing and attribution. In 133 adults given CD19 CAR T cells, Gust et al. found that those with severe neurotoxicity had endothelial activation (disseminated intravascular coagulation, capillary leak) and increased blood-brain barrier permeability, and that the permeable barrier failed to protect the cerebrospinal fluid from high systemic cytokine concentrations including interferon-gamma. Higher risk went with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, high marrow CD19-positive burden, high CAR T-cell dose, CRS and pre-existing neurological disease, and markers of endothelial activation before lymphodepletion were higher in people who later had grade 4 or worse neurotoxicity. That is an association in one product class and population, not a complete mechanism for every treatment. ICANS can accompany CRS or follow its own timetable, and neurotoxicity after CRS is scored separately, so recovery of blood pressure and oxygen does not show neurological recovery. If a person is confused while taking a sedating medicine and the ICE score falls, the grading rule requires that sedation be excluded, so the fall calls for clinical assessment, neither ignored nor diagnosed from the score alone. Clinical assessment also considers infection, metabolic disturbances, medicines and pre-existing neurologic disease. A safety report should retain onset, severity, attributed cause, interventions, duration, recovery and how many people were adequately observed. Separate fictional CRS and neurologic timelines can end at different times; they do not specify a typical order or duration. Stopping an engineered input does not guarantee immediate reversal of established neurologic injury.

fields.before: Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) are the autoimmune side effects of Immune checkpoint inhibitors, including colitis, thyroid problems, rash, hepatitis and pneumonitis. Any organ can be affected, and they are most frequent and most severe when CTLA-4 and PD-1 blockade are combined. Management relies on steroids and biologics; some irAEs, notably the endocrinopathies, are permanent, and their occurrence correlates only weakly with response. The term is cited by the Melanoma and Mesothelioma entries and the drug records for Toripalimab, Tislelizumab and Camrelizumab, by the bottlenecks on toxicity and on predicting immunotherapy response, and by ideas on testing drugs in old and unhealthy animals and reading the immune response in blood three weeks in.
fields.after:
Immune-related adverse events are injuries attributed to treatment-related immune activity, commonly discussed with checkpoint inhibitors. They can affect the bowel, lung, skin, liver, hormone-producing glands and other organs. A symptom or laboratory change during treatment does not by itself establish an immune cause.

Clinical assessment identifies the organ, severity, timing and competing explanations. Reactions can arise after treatment stops, and some endocrine injury leaves lasting loss of function. Organ-specific management can include different measures, such as treatment interruption, immunosuppression or hormone replacement. An adverse event, an attributed immune injury and a cancer-response result are separate findings.

before: Pembrolizumab before and after surgery for triple-negative breast cancer: Macmillan says the treatment can make the immune system too active, that side effects can start during treatment or after it ends, and that glands making hormones (such as the thyroid) can be permanently affected, sometimes needing daily tablets. The symptoms both charities ask you to report straight away on the 24-hour number: more stools than usual, stools at night, watery stools or tummy cramps (bowel inflammation); breathlessness, a cough that does not go away, wheeze or fever (lung inflammation); yellow skin or eyes, sickness (liver inflammation); unusual tiredness, headaches that do not go away, dizziness, thirst or passing more urine (hormone glands).

Lung cancer: checkpoint treatment is used at every stage of lung cancer, so the same warning list applies whether it is given before surgery, after chemoradiotherapy or for cancer that has spread. Macmillan says to contact the hospital straight away on the 24-hour number for breathlessness, a cough that does not go away, wheezing or a fever over 37.5 C (lung inflammation); for passing more stools than is normal for you or passing stools at night (bowel inflammation); for a spreading rash, blistering or peeling skin with flu-like symptoms; and for a temperature above 37.5 C or below 36 C or feeling unwell with a normal temperature. It also says these can start during treatment or after treatment ends, which is why the patient alert card is worth carrying.
after: What the label does and does not say. An adverse event is any unfavourable and unintended sign, symptom or abnormal laboratory finding that occurs during treatment, whether or not the treatment caused it; grading records that it occurred and how severe it was, and the clinical team assigns attribution to the drug, the intervention or something else (NCI Cancer Therapy Evaluation Program). An irAE is the narrower attribution of harm to treatment-related immune activity, so a symptom during immunotherapy is not automatically an irAE, and the abbreviation names a suspected mechanism, not an organ, a severity or a treatment. The SITC 2021 guideline uses the same wording, grades events including irAEs on a scale such as CTCAE version 5, and says that some irAEs need organ-specific management while overarching principles apply to all checkpoint-inhibitor toxicity. Checkpoint regulation helps limit responses against healthy tissue, part of peripheral tolerance; disrupting that protection can contribute to immune injury, but no single mechanism explains every event. Colitis names bowel inflammation and pneumonitis lung inflammation. A symptom or the suffix "-itis" does not establish its cause.

Timing and neighbouring syndromes. Immune-mediated reactions to PD-1 or PD-L1 antibodies can occur in any organ system at any time after starting and can also appear after treatment stops (pembrolizumab prescribing information), so the infusion calendar does not define the observation window; onset differs by organ, with a SITC median of 5 to 10 weeks for diarrhoea or colitis and rash typically presenting 2 to 5 weeks after the first treatment. Cytokine release syndrome and ICANS after immune effector cell therapy are separate syndromes with their own ASTCT definitions and grading, not substitute labels for checkpoint-related organ injury, and stopping a treatment does not guarantee the immune effect has stopped.

Report symptoms using the care team's plan and tell evaluating clinicians about current and previous immunotherapy. New or worsening breathing difficulty, chest pain or confusion can need urgent assessment. A person with a new cough after checkpoint treatment should neither dismiss the possible relationship because dosing ended nor infer pneumonitis without evaluation. The organ-inflammation guidance from NCI advises reporting concerning changes rather than waiting for another infusion or starting immune-suppressing treatment independently. Suspected immune injury does not show that the cancer treatment is working.

fields.before: An adverse event is anything bad that happens to a patient during a trial, whether or not the drug caused it; a side effect is a harm the drug is known to cause. Trial tables list adverse events and then judge which were treatment-related.
fields.after: An adverse event is an unwanted medical occurrence recorded during treatment or follow-up, whether or not treatment caused it; occurrence, severity and attribution are separate findings.

fields.before: Counting every adverse event, including those from the cancer itself or from unrelated illness, is deliberate: it avoids under-reporting and lets the two arms be compared fairly, since the control arm has adverse events too. Investigators then attribute each event as related or unrelated to treatment, yielding 'treatment-related adverse events', and grade its severity; drug labels list the side effects seen more often on the drug than on placebo. Some harms appear only years later (heart damage from anthracyclines, second cancers after radiation, permanent hormone deficiencies after immunotherapy) and are called late effects, and survivorship care exists to watch for them.
fields.after:
An adverse event can be an unfavourable sign, including an abnormal laboratory finding, symptom or disease temporally associated with a treatment or intervention. Recording it does not establish causation. Investigators separately assess severity and how likely it is to be related to treatment.

A treatment-related adverse reaction is a more specific attribution. Safety comparisons should retain the event definition, population, observation window, denominator and attribution method. Seriousness is a separate reporting category and is not interchangeable with a severity grade. Some harms first arise or persist after treatment ends, so an administration calendar does not define the entire safety window.

after: Name the scale and its version when reading a grade. CTCAE bands changed between versions (see the summary), and some toxicities of immune effector cell therapy have their own consensus scales: in the ASTCT 2019 consensus, cytokine release syndrome and ICANS are graded on ASTCT tables, while organ toxicities associated with CRS may be graded on CTCAE version 5.0 but do not change the CRS grade, and tremor and myoclonus may be graded on CTCAE but do not change the ICANS grade. A trial report should therefore say which scale and which version it used before its grades are compared with another trial's.

The general CTCAE descriptions run from grade 1, mild, through grade 2, moderate, grade 3, severe or medically significant, grade 4, life-threatening, and grade 5, death related to the event. Not every grade is defined for every event. Seriousness is a separate reporting concept: a grade is not an attribution to the drug or a substitute for the event's specific criteria. Immune-effector syndromes can use ASTCT scales instead, so do not apply a generic five-grade ladder to every syndrome.

after: Reading a neutrophil count. The absolute neutrophil count (ANC) is the number of neutrophils per volume of blood, written as cells per microlitre or as times 10 to the ninth per litre; it is more specific than the total white cell count, which includes other cell types. One ANC is a snapshot. Two invented curves make the point: both read 0.5 times 10 to the ninth per litre on day 3, but in one the count dips briefly and recovers, while in the other it stays at that level from day 2 to day 4. The matching number does not mean matching risk, because depth, duration and trend matter, and a count alone neither establishes nor excludes infection. Keep the sampling date, units, the laboratory's reference range and the place in the treatment cycle with the number. NCI patient guidance lists a temperature of 38 degrees Celsius or higher among the signs of infection to report promptly, whatever an earlier count showed. Better counts and fewer infections are related but separate outcomes, and neither is tumour response.

For a prevention study, retain the actual anticancer regimen, risk factors, comparator, fever-and-count definition and observation window. A toxicity report needs its count threshold and grading version. The same ANC on one date can conceal different durations of low counts, and an earlier reassuring count does not dismiss new fever or other infection symptoms. Supportive-care benefit, such as fewer infections, is distinct from cancer control.

fields.before: How a drug moves through the body: how much is absorbed, how high the blood level gets, how long it lasts (half-life) and how it is cleared. These numbers decide the dose, the schedule and whether a pill can be taken with food or other medicines.
fields.after: Pharmacokinetics follows a named medicine or its components through the body by measuring concentration over time, which differs from both the amount administered and the biological effect.

fields.before: Antibodies have half-lives of 2-4 weeks and are dosed every 2-6 weeks, often now at flat doses (pembrolizumab 400 mg q6w) rather than by weight; small molecules are dosed daily and interact with CYP3A4 inhibitors, acid suppressants and food; chemotherapy is dosed by body surface area with organ-function adjustments. Exposure-response analyses link drug levels to efficacy and toxicity and underpin Project Optimus's push to find optimal rather than maximal doses; therapeutic drug monitoring is used for busulfan, methotrexate and increasingly for TKIs. Radiopharmaceutical PK determines tumour versus kidney and marrow dose (dosimetry). Poor oral bioavailability has ended more than one promising drug's development.
fields.after:
Pharmacokinetics describes absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion. A dose is an administered amount; exposure describes a named substance's concentration over time in a specified compartment. Route, organ function, metabolism, binding and interactions can make equal doses produce different exposure.

The December 2016 FDA labelling guidance asks for measures such as maximum plasma concentration, concentration-time area under the curve, clearance, accumulation and half-life in their relevant conditions. These measurements inform dosage selection alongside activity, safety and tolerability; they do not establish benefit on their own. For conjugated drugs, active metabolites and radiopharmaceuticals, specify which component was measured. Blood concentration is not automatically the concentration of active material at a cancer-cell target.

after: Dose, exposure and effect are three different things. Dose is the administered amount; exposure is a named substance's concentration over time in a named place, which route, organ function, interactions and product properties can change for the same dose; and effect is a separate measurement, because effects or injury can persist after exposure falls and detectable drug does not guarantee productive engagement. Pharmacokinetics follows absorption (including how much of an oral dose reaches the circulation), distribution (plasma is not the unbound concentration inside a cell), metabolism (active metabolites may add their own exposure) and excretion, summarised by clearance, the removal relative to concentration, in volume per time. FDA labelling guidance lists the maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) and area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) at the approved dosage, time to steady state, accumulation ratio, clearance, volume of distribution and half-life; this AUC is an exposure area and is unrelated to the area under a prediction curve that judges tests.

For an antibody-drug conjugate, specify whether an assay follows conjugated antibody, total antibody, unconjugated payload or an active breakdown product. The 2024 FDA guidance defines total antibody as antibody with or without attached payload and discusses relevant constituent parts, metabolites and catabolites. Their concentration histories can differ: persistent antibody signal does not establish active payload in every cancer cell. Living cell products can expand or persist, and a radioligand combines radioactive decay with biological removal, so a freely circulating drug's half-life gives no universal clock for them.

Read the measurement card as well as the curve. Record the dose, route, analyte, sampled compartment, assay, population and sampling interval. Concentration can be in ng/mL, maximum concentration in the same units, concentration-time area in ng·hour/mL, half-life in hours and clearance in litres per hour. Sampling should capture the phase of interest: a sparse late sample cannot reliably recover an unobserved early peak. Pharmacodynamics measures biological effects separately. First-pass metabolism can reduce oral bioavailability; protein binding and active metabolites also matter.

The fictional halving example assumes one compartment, stopped input and a constant four-hour half-life. Its four markers are model values, not observed samples: 100, 50, 25 and 12.5 ng/mL at 0, 4, 8 and 12 hours. Integrating that exponential only from 0 to 12 hours gives about 505 ng·hour/mL, not the lifetime area, administered dose or biological effect. The example supplies no safe next-treatment time.

fields.before: The time it takes for the amount of a drug in the blood to fall by half. It sets how often a drug must be given: hours to a day for small molecules such as kinase inhibitors, so they are taken daily, and two to four weeks for antibodies, so they are given every three or six weeks.
fields.after: A half-life describes how long a specified drug concentration takes to fall by half under stated conditions; it does not by itself determine a treatment interval or when an effect ends.

fields.before: Small molecules are typically cleared by the liver and kidneys within hours to a day, so kinase inhibitors are taken daily; antibodies are protected from breakdown by recycling receptors and persist for two to four weeks, allowing dosing every three or six weeks. Half-life shapes both benefit and harm: a long-lived checkpoint inhibitor keeps working, and keeps causing immune side effects, for months after the last dose, while a radioactive drug's physical half-life (6.6 days for lutetium-177, 10 days for actinium-225) determines how long it irradiates the tumour. Pharmacokinetics is the study of these processes, and matching dose and schedule to them is central to dose optimisation.
fields.after:
A drug's half-life describes a halving of the concentration of a named substance in a specified phase or model. Early distribution, terminal elimination and the effective half-life relevant to accumulation can differ. With nonlinear elimination, a reported value can also depend on the dose. The December 2016 FDA clinical-pharmacology labelling guidance distinguishes effective from terminal half-life and asks for the conditions needed to interpret each.

Concentration and effect need separate measurements. Active metabolites, persistent biological changes and tissue injury can matter after the measured parent drug has declined. Living cell products can expand rather than simply disappear, and a radiopharmaceutical combines physical decay with biological removal. A half-life alone supplies no universal treatment schedule or recovery clock.

Dose intensity is the amount of a named medicine delivered per unit time, commonly milligrams per square metre per week. Relative dose intensity divides that by the intensity of a specified reference regimen. Illness and toxicity can drive both modification and outcomes, so an observational association is not a causal effect of changing the dose. Bonadonna and Valagussa's retrospective 1981 CMF analysis associated benefit with at least 85% of the planned dose in that regimen; this was a dose-level finding, not a universal relative-intensity threshold or proof for other treatments.

In the fictional four-dose example, both schedules use the same Drug Z and formulation. The first window is week 0 up to week 4, with administrations at weeks 0, 1, 2 and 3; the second is week 0 up to week 8, with administrations at weeks 0, 2, 4 and 6. Each declared window includes one nominal final interval and no administration at its right endpoint. Both totals are 40 arbitrary units, but the intensities are 10 and 5 units per week. A different final-cycle convention needs its own definition. Cumulative dose retains amount units; intensity adds a time denominator; relative intensity is the dimensionless ratio to a stated reference.

fields.before: Molecular pumps on cancer cells that eject chemotherapy and ADC payloads before they can act.
fields.after: An efflux pump moves particular substances out of cells. Some pumps can reduce exposure to chemotherapy drugs or released antibody-drug-conjugate payloads.

fields.before: Drug efflux pumps are ABC transporters on cancer cells that eject chemotherapy and ADC payloads before they can act. The main ones are ABCB1 (P-glycoprotein or MDR1), ABCG2 (BCRP) and ABCC1 (MRP1), with substrates including taxanes, anthracyclines, MMAE, DXd and, for ABCG2, SN-38. They are upregulated in mesenchymal and stem-like states, hence the term's place in the Epithelial-mesenchymal transition & drug efflux pathway; some newer payloads and radiation are efflux-independent, whereas pump inhibitors failed clinically because of toxicity. It is linked to the Antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) and Cytotoxic chemotherapy technologies, to the bottleneck Acquired resistance to every therapy, and to ideas on payload-class switching and efflux-agnostic therapy for mesenchymal TNBC.
fields.after:
Drug efflux pumps can export particular medicines or released antibody-drug-conjugate payloads that are their substrates. Important examples include ABCB1 (P-glycoprotein or MDR1), ABCG2 (BCRP) and ABCC1 (MRP1). The same transporter can handle several unrelated compounds, but a pump name does not establish that every medicine is a substrate.

Expression and transport activity are different measurements. A high RNA signal does not by itself show that enough active transporter reaches the membrane to alter drug exposure. Cell-line resistance and restoration by an inhibitor can support a mechanism in that model; they do not establish a validated clinical selection test or make switching payloads effective in every tumour.

after: How to read evidence about pumps. Pump RNA is not pump function: function depends on protein at the membrane and on whether a particular drug is a substrate. It is tested with fluorescent substrates that cells retain less when a pump is active, with and without an inhibitor, or by measuring intracellular drug; in SN-38-resistant breast and gastric cell lines, functional ABCG2 but not ABCB1 was found, and ABCG2 inhibitors restored SN-38 toxicity (Chang et al.). Substrate status is specific to each drug, so being pumped for one topoisomerase I payload does not establish it for another. A pump acts on a drug after it arrives and is not the drug's target, and a cell can keep an ADC's target protein, take the ADC up normally and still resist by exporting the released payload.

fields.before: Cancer cells can install pumps in their outer membrane that throw chemotherapy back out as fast as it comes in. The same pumps guard the gut, brain and bone marrow in healthy tissue, which is why blocking them failed as a strategy and why drug designers now choose payloads the pumps cannot grip.
fields.after: Drug transporters can lower cellular exposure to particular anticancer drugs. Their substrate profile, location and activity matter; expression alone does not select a treatment.

fields.before: ATP-binding cassette transporters, chiefly ABCB1 (P-glycoprotein/MDR1), ABCG2 (BCRP) and ABCC1 (MRP1), hydrolyse ATP to export hydrophobic drugs: taxanes, vinca alkaloids, anthracyclines, MMAE, DM1, several TKIs (ABCB1); SN-38, topotecan, mitoxantrone, methotrexate (ABCG2). They are constitutive in intestine, liver, kidney, the blood-brain barrier and stem cells (including leukaemia and cancer stem cells, the 'side population'), and are induced by EMT transcription factors, hypoxia, NRF2 (KEAP1-mutant tumours), and by drug exposure itself (ABCB1 amplification and promoter fusions in ovarian cancer after taxanes). Three generations of P-gp inhibitors (verapamil, valspodar, tariquidar) failed in phase 3 through pharmacokinetic interactions and lack of benefit. Modern responses: choose payloads that are poor substrates (DXd and exatecan are less affected than SN-38 and MMAE; PBD dimers; radionuclides are pump-independent), use ADCs to raise intracellular delivery, and exploit collateral sensitivity (pump-expressing cells are more sensitive to some agents). Efflux at the BBB limits CNS activity of most drugs; brain-penetrant TKIs are engineered to evade P-gp.
fields.after:
ATP-binding cassette transporters use ATP to move substrates across membranes. ABCB1, ABCG2 and ABCC1 can transport several anticancer drugs, with different substrate profiles. Their normal protective and excretory roles also affect absorption, distribution and drug interactions; transporter activity at the blood-brain or placental barrier is a different setting from activity in a cancer cell.

Acquired resistance can involve increased transport, but antigen loss, altered processing and other mechanisms must be assessed separately. Inhibiting a pump can change both tumour exposure and exposure in normal tissues. The unsuccessful clinical development of several P-glycoprotein inhibitors does not identify one universal reason for failure, and a resistant cell model does not itself select a treatment for a person.

after: Which pump handles which drug, and on what evidence. ABCG2 confers resistance to SN-38 and topotecan: in HEK-293 cells made to express wild-type or mutant ABCG2, cytotoxicity assays showed high resistance to mitoxantrone, SN-38 and topotecan and no appreciable resistance to etoposide or taxol (Robey et al. 2003), while in SN-38-resistant breast and gastric cell lines ABCG2 inhibitors restored SN-38 toxicity (Chang et al. 2016, SN-38 only). For P-gp, a brentuximab vedotin-resistant Hodgkin lymphoma line showed MMAE resistance and MDR1 upregulation, and 1 of 10 Hodgkin lymphoma patient samples expressed MDR1 (Chen et al.). Robey and colleagues' 2018 review describes ABCC1-mediated resistance to doxorubicin, etoposide and vincristine, transport of glutathione and glucuronide conjugates, and protective transporters at the brain and placental barriers. Zeng and colleagues' 2001 transport study also demonstrated MRP1 transport of methotrexate and folates, with polyglutamylation strongly limiting methotrexate transport. These are cell-line and overexpression models, not measurements of a tumour, and these laboratory findings do not validate a pump assay for selecting clinical therapy; Robey et al. 2018 describe efforts to make MDR1 a therapeutic target as unsuccessful so far. Normal-tissue protection also has experimental support: Zhou and colleagues found greater mitoxantrone sensitivity in Bcrp1-deficient mouse haematopoietic cells than in wild-type cells, supporting a protective role in that model. Robey's review also describes gastrointestinal transport affecting oral availability. These normal-tissue roles should not be confused with a cancer-specific mechanism.

Antibody-drug conjugates meet pumps after delivery. Direct transport by an efflux pump concerns a released payload that is its substrate, rather than export of the intact antibody-drug conjugate during endocytosis; A neighbouring cell could likewise export a payload that entered it, but a reduced bystander effect is a mechanistic hypothesis here, not a demonstrated clinical result. The absence of this efflux mechanism does not prove that delivery, release or target action succeeded; other barriers can remain. In breast cancer cells made resistant to trastuzumab deruxtecan or sacituzumab govitecan, resistance was mainly payload-specific, notably more efflux-transporter activity rather than loss of antigen, and ADCs with microtubule-inhibitor payloads restored activity in cells and animals (Rampa et al.); exatecan conjugates with a traceless self-immolative linker moiety overcame resistance of DXd and SN-38 conjugates in multidrug-resistance-positive models (Weng et al.). A study could compare intact ADC and free payload on the same cells, with and without a pump inhibitor, to ask which delivery step is affected. That comparison would still need controls for the inhibitor's other effects.

fields.before: The gap between the dose that works and the dose that harms. Classic chemotherapy has a narrow window (the dose that kills the tumour nearly kills the patient); a wider window is the whole point of targeted drugs, ADCs and immunotherapy.
fields.after: Therapeutic index is a ratio comparing doses that produce defined toxic and useful effects; a therapeutic window is a range, and neither is a personal guarantee of safety.

fields.before: Toxicity can be on-target (the drug hits its intended molecule in normal tissue that also expresses it: EGFR inhibitors and skin, HER2 and heart, CD19 CAR-T and normal B cells, 'on-target off-tumour') or off-target (unintended molecules: hERG and QT prolongation, kinase promiscuity). ADCs widen the window by delivering payloads selectively, but the payload's free fraction sets their class effects (ILD for deruxtecan, ocular toxicity for MMAF, neuropathy for MMAE). Dose-finding in phase 1 traditionally sought the maximum tolerated dose; Project Optimus reframes it as finding the dose with the best therapeutic index, and tolerability over months of continuous therapy is now recognised as part of efficacy.
fields.after:
A formal therapeutic index divides a dose producing a specified toxic effect by a dose producing a specified useful effect in stated experimental conditions. It is dimensionless when the dose units are compatible. A therapeutic window instead describes a range of doses or concentrations meeting stated activity and harm criteria. Always retain the effect definitions, population, time and uncertainty.

Low-concentration activity, target binding or a wider margin in a laboratory assay does not establish clinical safety. Distribution, formulation, schedule, other medicines and longer-term effects can change the relationship. The August 2024 FDA oncology dosage-optimisation guidance considers exposure, activity, safety and tolerability together, rather than assuming that the highest tolerated dose must be optimal. Its scope is stated for particular development settings and does not supply one rule for every treatment modality.

after: A laboratory margin depends on which useful and harmful effects were tested, in which populations and over what time. A measure built on one toxicity can miss another. Different conditions in tumour-cell and normal-cell assays also limit transfer to people. A more selective result in one pair of cultures supports that assay comparison, not a general clinical safety claim. FDA's narrow-therapeutic-index discussion concerns small changes in dose or concentration causing treatment failure or serious harm; it does not classify all chemotherapy as one regulatory group.

Payload and loading change the margin. In one mouse study of anti-CD30 MMAE conjugates with 2, 4 or 8 drugs per antibody, the 4-loaded conjugate's antitumour activity matched the 8-loaded at equal antibody dose, the maximum tolerated dose of the 2-loaded was at least double that of the 4-loaded, which was twice that of the 8-loaded, and the 8-loaded cleared 3-fold faster than the 4-loaded; lower loading raised the therapeutic index for that conjugate (Hamblett et al.), which does not generalise to every ADC. FDA's August 2024 oncology dosage-optimisation guidance integrates exposure, activity, safety and tolerability, and says it does not specifically address radiopharmaceuticals, cellular and gene therapy products, oncolytic viruses, microbiota or cancer vaccines, or paediatric development.

A complete fictional ratio example specifies the same model-organism population, one administration and day-14 readouts. Useful effect is an invented decrease of at least two points on a 0-to-10 symptom score; toxicity is an injury marker at least twice baseline. Constructed curves reach 50% at doses 2 and 6, giving an index of 6/2 = 3. Separate, arbitrarily chosen criteria of at least 80% meeting the useful readout and at most 10% meeting the toxic readout give a dose range of about 2.83 to 3.46 on those curves. The range keeps dose units and depends on its criteria. No sampling uncertainty or acceptable clinical harm threshold is supplied.

fields.before: Trial-design vocabulary: the backbone is the established treatment everyone in the trial receives; the add-on is the new drug tested on top of it; monotherapy means the drug alone. Most modern approvals are add-ons to a backbone.
fields.after: A backbone is the reference treatment in a combination comparison, an add-on is tested with it, and monotherapy uses one treatment; the comparison must establish what the combination adds in benefit and harm.

fields.before: Testing a new drug added to standard therapy (backbone) versus the backbone alone is the fastest route to approval because it needs no head-to-head against the standard, but it means patients receive more drugs and more toxicity, and it can obscure whether the new agent could replace rather than supplement (the 'chemotherapy-free' question in CLL, lung cancer and myeloma). Single-agent activity in early trials (objective response rate as monotherapy) is the usual evidence that a drug contributes. Regulators sometimes require 'contribution of components' studies when a combination is approved without it.
fields.after:
A trial can compare a reference regimen, often called the backbone, with that regimen plus another treatment. Monotherapy studies a treatment on its own. Name the disease, prior treatment, components, doses, schedule, comparator and outcome before interpreting what the result establishes.

A combination that outperforms A alone has not thereby shown superiority to B alone or identified a synergistic interaction. Component contributions, added toxicity and changes in exposure or deliverability require their own evidence. A proposed mechanism can motivate a comparison, but the clinical result and its uncertainty determine the conclusion supported in that setting.

after: Reading a combination result. A combination rationale should name the job of each component (for example a growth pathway, a survival route, a location or stage, or a resistant population), and each story makes predictions that need testing. A regimen that beats one component does not show which component supplied the benefit, nor superiority to every alternative. In ASCENT-04 (443 people with previously untreated locally advanced or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer whose tumours express PD-L1, combined positive score 10 or higher), median progression-free survival was 11.2 months with sacituzumab govitecan plus pembrolizumab and 7.8 months with physician's-choice chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab (hazard ratio 0.65, 95 per cent CI 0.51 to 0.84; label section 14); that compares the ADC with chemotherapy as pembrolizumab's partner and does not by itself show synergy. Independent drug action offers another explanation: if each person benefits from the drug to which their tumour is most sensitive, patient-to-patient variability alone can explain the superiority of many approved combinations without additivity or synergy (Palmer and Sorger), which is an alternative explanation, not a rule that effective combinations lack synergy. A combination can also add toxicity, change exposure or force lower doses, and simultaneous and sequential treatment are different strategies that a molecular diagram cannot choose between.

What 'synergy' means and how it is measured. Synergy is the narrower claim that a combined effect exceeds a stated reference expectation, and the references differ. Highest single agent (Gaddum) expects the better single effect and is the easiest bar to clear. Bliss independence expects the probability of being unaffected by each drug to be independent, so for effects written as fractions the expectation is A plus B minus A times B. Loewe additivity treats the two drugs as dilutions of one another and needs the full dose-response curve of each, with straight-line isoboles as its classic form. In Chou's median-effect method a combination index below 1 indicates synergism, equal to 1 additivity and above 1 antagonism, within that method only. Meyer et al. found no consensus on how to quantify synergy, and Yadav et al. note that a drug combined with itself can easily exceed the highest single agent and that their zero-interaction potency score is zero when both independence and dose additivity hold. A 2020 review's point stands: a synergy claim needs its model, scale and uncertainty named. Greco's 1995 review was identified but only its title could be read. Laboratory interaction analysis needs single-drug dose-response data, combination conditions, controls and variation estimates; a clinical survival advantage does not by itself measure a cell-level interaction.

The two fictional comparisons use different units of inference. In a ten-tumour better-component model, A covers tumours 1 to 4 and B covers 3 to 6: 4 + 4 - 2 = 6 in the union, with four in neither group. There is no extra within-tumour interaction or added toxicity in that counting model. Separately, one cultured-cell experiment at 72 hours gives 20%, 30% and 40% inhibition for A, B and the pair at one fixed dose pair. Inhibition here is a reduction in vehicle-normalised viable-cell count, not a direct death measurement. HSA expects 30% and Bliss 44%, so 40% exceeds the first and falls below the second. Loewe needs single-drug dose-response curves; three numbers and no uncertainty estimate cannot establish a general synergy claim. In this model, greater overlap among responders reduces the union. Independent drug action does not require the two response groups to be statistically independent; shared resistance and response correlation matter to a population prediction.

fields.before: Two genes where losing either alone is fine but losing both kills the cell. Cancers that have lost one become vulnerable to drugs against the other.
fields.after: Synthetic lethality means that two impairments together kill a cell even though either alone is tolerated; finding one genetic change does not establish that a particular drug will produce that interaction.

fields.before: Synthetic lethality describes two genes where losing either alone is tolerated but losing both kills the cell, so a cancer that has lost one becomes vulnerable to a drug against the other. BRCA and PARP is the proven pair; others in development include MTAP/PRMT5, MSI/WRN, HRD/POLQ, TP53/WEE1, SMARCA4/SMARCA2 and ARID1A/EZH2, and CRISPR screens map such pairs systematically. The concept links to the Synthetic lethality approaches, PARP inhibitors and CRISPR functional genomics technologies and is cited by the Ovarian cancer and Mesothelioma entries, The Institute of Cancer Research and Christopher Lord. Ideas drawing on it include PRMT5/MAT2A lethality for MTAP-deleted mesothelioma, a WRN inhibitor programme and a synthetic lethality map for every cancer driver.
fields.after:
Synthetic lethality is a lethal interaction between two impairments, each of which can be tolerated alone in the tested system. One impairment may already be present in a cancer and an experimental intervention can create the second, so the concept does not require two drugs. Genetic identity, loss of function, target engagement and the lethal outcome each need evidence.

The 2005 Farmer and Bryant studies found sensitivity to PARP inhibition in BRCA-impaired experimental systems. Murai and colleagues later distinguished PARP trapping from catalytic inhibition. These findings support particular mechanisms; they do not make every BRCA-related finding a clinical selection rule. Candidate pairs such as MTAP with PRMT5, mismatch-repair deficiency with WRN, or repair deficiency with POLQ need their own model, exposure, selectivity and clinical evidence.

after: What has to be shown. Compare matched cells with neither impairment, each alone and both, and check that the intended functions changed. Measure death separately from slower growth, because a viability signal can fall when cells divide less or change metabolism; pair a suitable death assay with long-term survival or colony formation, and record concentration, time and denominator, remembering that colony formation measures reproductive survival and not the way cells die. Synthetic lethality is not oncogene addiction, which is dependence on an active driver: in Src-, BCR-ABL- and EGF receptor-dependent cells, unequal attenuation of survival and pro-apoptotic signals after the driver is inactivated contributes to death (Sharma et al.). It is also not synergy, since a score above a reference model does not identify which losses interact. In the BRCA/PARP example, homologous recombination is a DNA repair process and HRD means deficiency of that process. Trapping PARP on DNA and inhibiting its catalytic activity are different perturbations, while repair restoration or changes in replication stress can change sensitivity. The first impairment can pre-exist, so a two-loss interaction does not require two drugs.

Rescue, restoration and what each test can show. A rescue experiment restores a relevant function and asks whether the predicted harm falls; that strengthens attribution, but a failed rescue is not automatic disproof, because the restored function may not be expressed, localised or timed adequately (a reading rule, not a result from these experiments). A real example of functional restoration involved secondary BRCA2 mutations, often described as reversions. Ovarian cancer lines PEO1, PEO4 and PEO6 came from one BRCA2 mutation carrier: PEO1 was BRCA2 deficient and sensitive to cisplatin and a PARP inhibitor, while a secondary BRCA2 mutation that cancelled the inherited one arose in the patient (PEO4, PEO6) and, under cisplatin and PARP-inhibitor selection of PEO1, in the dish, restoring BRCA2 and resistance. Function was shown by homologous recombination assays after transfecting wild-type or mutant BRCA2 cDNA into reporter cells, and transient siRNA depletion (two siRNAs against a non-targeting control) re-sensitised the restored clones and PEO4 (Sakai et al. 2009). That is a secondary-mutation restoration plus knockdown in one patient's lineage, not a designed rescue of a knockout, and depleting a protein is not the same as inhibiting it with a drug. BRCA and PARP evidence is experimental: BRCA1 or BRCA2 dysfunction sensitised cells to PARP inhibition (Farmer et al.), BRCA2-deficient cells and tumours were acutely sensitive (Bryant et al.), and PARP inhibitors trap PARP1 and PARP2 on damaged DNA, with trapping potency (niraparib above olaparib, far above veliparib) not tracking catalytic inhibition (Murai et al.). Normal tissue can share the vulnerability: normal Brca2-deficient mouse intestinal epithelium showed very high apoptosis within hours of PARP inhibition (Hay et al.). None of this establishes clinical benefit.

A fictional test uses matched cultures over the same interval: neither impairment, A alone, B alone and A plus B. Each single impairment is tolerated and only the pair causes death measured by a validated assay, with independent perturbations reproducing it. In a separate rescue culture, restoring A while B remains impaired reduces death; this tests attribution and does not revive already dead cells. If a short assay instead shows fewer cells, slower division and cell loss remain unresolved. Other cell backgrounds and normal cells are separate tests of context and selectivity.

after: A wide therapeutic window is a design hope for each candidate pair, not a property shown for all of them: in mice, normal Brca2-deficient intestinal epithelium was highly sensitive to PARP inhibition (Hay et al.). A candidate needs lethality of the pair with each single loss tolerated, death shown by a validated assay and not only fewer cells, independent perturbations, and a rescue or restoration test, with the limits of each stated.

fields.before: A small molecule drug is a chemically made medicine small enough to slip inside cells, so it can usually be taken as a tablet.
fields.after: Small-molecule medicines can act on intracellular targets, but size alone does not establish cell entry, oral absorption, selectivity or safety.

fields.before:
A small molecule is a drug built by chemical synthesis rather than grown in living cells. Its molecules are hundreds of times lighter than an antibody, which lets them cross cell membranes and reach targets inside the cell, such as kinases, DNA repair enzymes and survival proteins. Most kinase inhibitors, PARP inhibitors, BCL2 inhibitors and hormone blockers are small molecules, and so is almost every classic chemotherapy drug.

Because they are stable and absorbed from the gut, small molecules are usually tablets or capsules taken at home, which is why so much of modern targeted therapy is oral. The trade-offs are the flip side of the same chemistry: they are cleared by liver enzymes, so food and other medicines can change their levels; they can bind related proteins and cause off-target side effects; and a single mutation in the target can stop them binding, which is a common route to resistance.

The other big class is biologics: antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates, bispecifics and cell therapies. These are made in cells, given by infusion or injection, and act mainly on targets at the cell surface or in the blood. Many treatment plans combine both, for example a small-molecule inhibitor with an antibody, or chemotherapy with a checkpoint inhibitor. The rule-of-thumb properties that predict whether a small molecule will be absorbed by mouth were set out by Lipinski and by Veber, and still guide drug design.
fields.after:
Many small-molecule medicines can reach targets inside cells, such as kinases and DNA-repair enzymes. Their actual entry, distribution, unbound concentration, metabolism and export depend on the compound and the system. Some are taken by mouth and others are administered by injection; formulation and clinical pharmacology must be checked for the named product.

The National Cancer Institute distinguishes small-molecule and antibody-based targeted therapies and describes several different mechanisms. A treatment can act on more than one protein, and a target alteration can affect activity or resistance. A chemically defined molecule is not automatically selective, orally available or a useful research probe. Probe fitness, target engagement, functional consequences and clinical benefit require different evidence.

after: Why ADC side effects follow the payload more than the target. Payload can reach healthy cells by early release from an unstable linker, by antigen-independent uptake (pinocytosis), or by the target sitting on healthy tissue; the Drago review concludes that off-target, off-tumour adverse events appear to dominate the toxicity profiles of most existing ADCs, while giving true on-target examples. Those are patterns within published data with non-uniform reporting, and each product's own label governs its figures.

What the current labels report for the breast cancer products. Sacituzumab govitecan (SN-38 payload): neutropenia 64 per cent (grade 3 to 4, 48 per cent; febrile 6 per cent) and diarrhoea 62 per cent (grade 3 to 4, 10 per cent), with higher risk of neutropenia, febrile neutropenia and anaemia in people homozygous for UGT1A1*28. fields.before: The drugs that stopped chemotherapy from meaning days of vomiting: 5-HT3 blockers (ondansetron, palonosetron), NK1 blockers (aprepitant), dexamethasone and olanzapine, given by the emetic risk of each regimen.
fields.after: Antiemetic medicines prevent or treat nausea and vomiting. The preventive plan depends on the treatment's emetic risk and the person's circumstances.

fields.before: Before 1991, cisplatin caused vomiting in nearly all patients; ondansetron (1991), granisetron, palonosetron (2003, long-acting), aprepitant (2003, NK1 antagonist), fosaprepitant, netupitant-palonosetron (2014), rolapitant and olanzapine (Navari, NEJM 2016) built the modern regimen. Guidelines (MASCC/ESMO, ASCO, NCCN) classify regimens as high (cisplatin, AC), moderate, low or minimal emetic risk and prescribe three- or four-drug prophylaxis for high risk (NK1 + 5-HT3 + dexamethasone ± olanzapine). Breakthrough, anticipatory and radiation-induced nausea have separate algorithms. CINV remains under-treated in ~30% of patients, particularly delayed nausea; dexamethasone-sparing and lower-dose olanzapine (5 mg) are recent refinements.
fields.after:
Antiemetic medicines are used to prevent or treat nausea and vomiting, which are separate outcomes. Options include serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonists, neurokinin-1 receptor antagonists, dexamethasone and olanzapine. The regimen-specific guidance from MASCC and ESMO and the NCI PDQ describes combinations chosen for the emetic risk of the anticancer treatment and the clinical setting. A list of drug classes does not determine an individual medicine schedule.

Acute, delayed, anticipatory and breakthrough symptoms describe different timing or circumstances. Prevention differs from treatment of symptoms that have already appeared. Trials must state whether their endpoint is nausea, vomiting or a composite such as no vomiting and no rescue medication; meeting that composite does not establish that the person had no nausea.

after: Nausea and vomiting are different outcomes. Nausea is the sensation and vomiting the expulsion; they often occur together but one can occur without the other. Serotonin acting at 5-HT3 receptors and substance P acting at NK1 receptors contribute with other transmitters, and in two phase II cisplatin studies serotonin appeared to dominate early vomiting and substance P the later phase, with overlap (Hesketh et al.), so acute and delayed are reporting windows and not sealed pathways. It lists other causes too, such as fluid and electrolyte imbalance including hypercalcaemia or volume depletion, and tells clinicians to consider all potential causes when people receive several treatments, so new nausea needs a cause assessment.

Reading antiemetic trials. In Navari et al. (380 evaluable chemotherapy-naive adults given cisplatin at 70 mg per square metre or more, or cyclophosphamide-doxorubicin, all with dexamethasone, an NK1 antagonist and a 5-HT3 antagonist), nausea prevention was the primary endpoint and complete response (no emesis and no rescue medication) a secondary one. No nausea in the first 24 hours was 74 per cent with olanzapine against 45 per cent with placebo, while complete response was 86 per cent against 65 per cent, so a complete response does not mean no nausea, and a person with no vomiting can still have persistent nausea. MASCC and ESMO updated their regimen-specific guideline in 2023 (Herrstedt et al., published 2024). Read patient-reported nausea severity, vomiting episodes, rescue-medication use and the observation window together with the preventive regimen and adherence; symptoms that limit drinking or eating warrant prompt contact with the care team. This describes how to read endpoints, not a medicine schedule.

Gut-to-brain nerve signalling, blood-borne inputs and learned associations can contribute, so one blocked route does not account for every symptom. The timing terms organise observations. Acute commonly refers to the first 24 hours, delayed to symptoms beyond 24 hours, anticipatory to symptoms before treatment associated with previous experiences, and breakthrough to symptoms despite prevention. Learned symptoms are real; delayed does not mean mild, and early and later responses can overlap with multiday treatment. Prevention and treatment of symptoms that have appeared are different questions. In a fictional trial, no vomiting and no rescue medicine can meet its complete-response endpoint while the participant still reports nausea. fields.after: Insertional mutagenesis is a change in a cell's genes caused by added genetic material landing in its DNA and disrupting a gene or its control, and neither an insertion nor a growing cell clone shows by itself that a cancer has formed or what caused it.

Some gene delivery systems, including the viral vectors used to make engineered T cells and to correct inherited immune disorders in blood stem cells, insert a genetic cassette into the cell's genome. Integration is the event; insertional mutagenesis is a consequential change that the event causes, such as interrupting a gene or altering the activity of a nearby one. Integration alone does not establish a harmful biological consequence. A cell that gains a growth advantage passes the insertion to its descendants and a clone expands, but a growing clone is not a diagnosis of cancer, because a useful therapeutic response can also expand a clone. FDA's long-term follow-up guidance for gene therapy (January 2020) explains why the question is taken seriously: the biological activity of retroviral vectors and transposon elements is imparted by an integration event, such integration is in general not directed to specific sites, and that raises the potential for disruption of critical host genes or activation of proto-oncogenes near the site, and so the risk of malignancy. A nonviral transposon is therefore also an integrating system, and genome editing can produce its own undesirable changes with a risk of malignancy, which is a separate mechanism from vector insertion.

Three primary reports show why the setting matters. After retrovirus-mediated gamma-c gene transfer into autologous CD34-positive bone marrow cells for X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency, 9 of 10 patients were corrected, but almost three years later the two youngest developed uncontrolled clonal proliferation of mature T cells; both clones carried vector integration near the LMO2 proto-oncogene promoter with abnormal LMO2 expression, which the authors attributed most likely to retrovirus enhancer activity (Hacein-Bey-Abina et al., 2003). In a patient with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia given CD19 CAR T cells, 94 per cent of CAR T cells at the peak of response came from one clone in which lentiviral insertion had disrupted TET2, the patient's second TET2 allele carried a hypomorphic mutation, and the clone showed a central memory phenotype alongside complete remission: an expanded clone linked to benefit, not a new cancer (Fraietta et al., 2018). In 724 patients treated with T-cell therapies at one centre, a lethal T-cell lymphoma followed axicabtagene ciloleucel for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma; the tumour, the CAR T cells and the patient's normal blood cells were profiled in depth, both lymphomas were Epstein-Barr virus positive and linked to DNMT3A and TET2 mutant clonal haematopoiesis, and no evidence of oncogenic retroviral integration was found with multiple techniques (Hamilton et al., 2024). The first is a specific stem-cell regimen and the others are single-centre or single-patient observations, so none is an incidence estimate for a vector or product.

What regulators ask for follows from this. The August 2026 ABECMA prescribing information carries a boxed warning that T-cell malignancies, including CAR-positive tumours, have occurred after BCMA- and CD19-directed genetically modified autologous T-cell immunotherapies for blood cancers, may present within weeks of infusion and may be fatal, and says to monitor life-long for secondary malignancies. FDA's CAR T-cell development guidance recommends following people for 15 years after treatment with CAR T cells containing an integrated transgene, because integrating vectors may increase the risk of delayed adverse events and non-integrating vectors are thought to carry a low delayed risk. These are class-level product warnings and follow-up expectations; they do not assign one mechanism to every event or give an incidence for other products.

To attribute a malignancy after engineered-cell therapy, investigators ask whether the therapeutic sequence is present in the malignant cells, where the integrations are, whether they alter relevant genes, whether related clones were detectable earlier, and what prior therapy, underlying disease and pre-existing genetic changes contribute. Integration-site sequencing maps insertion locations, quantitative DNA assays estimate vector copies per cell, and flow cytometry, gene-expression measurement and pathology answer different questions about identity, function and malignancy; the sample is consumed by testing. Average vector copy number cannot show the position or effect of each insertion, a clone's frequency depends on the sampled cells, assay sensitivity and time, and blood may not represent every tissue. This record gives no copy-number or clone-frequency threshold because none of the sources read sets one. Messenger RNA delivery that does not integrate does not use genomic insertion as its route, which does not remove its other risks.

fields.after: On-target, off-tumour toxicity is harm to healthy tissue that carries the same target a treatment was built to recognise, so accurate recognition injures the tissue as well as the cancer.

On-target, off-tumour toxicity is injury from recognition of the intended target on healthy tissue. It differs from recognition of an unintended molecular target. The predictable, lymphoma-specific consequences of aiming at lineage antigens (B-cell aplasia, low immunoglobulin, and the effects of CD52, CCR4 and CD47 targeting) are described in the record on the cost of aiming at a lineage antigen, which this record does not repeat.

Many candidate cancer targets are normal proteins found at different levels or places in the body, so tumour-associated does not mean tumour-exclusive. A treatment that recognises its intended target wherever it is accessible, such as a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell, can harm any healthy tissue that displays it, and tissue location, target density, receptor properties and exposure all shape the outcome. This differs from off-target cross-reactivity, in which the receptor recognises an unintended molecule, and from cytokine release syndrome, which is systemic inflammatory activation; the three can occur together. It also differs from payload toxicity in an antibody-drug conjugate: a pooled analysis of ADC trials found the key grade 3 to 4 toxicities grouped by payload and concluded they were likely off-target and related to the payload (Masters et al., 2018). Binding specificity is not tissue selectivity, and experience with an antibody against a target does not automatically carry over to a living cell with a different recognition and signalling system.

Two primary reports show the contrast. A patient with colon cancer metastatic to the lungs and liver received 10 billion autologous T cells expressing a trastuzumab-based CAR against ERBB2 (HER2), the largest number permitted in the first dose-escalation cohort, the day after a lymphodepleting regimen of cyclophosphamide (60 mg/kg daily for 2 days) and fludarabine (25 mg/m2 for 5 days). Within 15 minutes the patient had respiratory distress, chest imaging showed pulmonary oedema, and the patient died 5 days after treatment, with marked rises in interferon-gamma, GM-CSF, tumour necrosis factor-alpha, interleukin-6 and interleukin-10. At autopsy multiple organs showed systemic ischaemia and haemorrhagic microangiopathic injury and the lungs diffuse alveolar damage; histological examination of autopsy tissue found ERBB2 at 3+ in liver metastases and 2+ in lung metastases and much lower levels in normal lung parenchyma, normal liver and normal breast. The authors hypothesised that highly active ERBB2-directed T cells recognised ERBB2 on normal lung cells on first pass through the lung and released inflammatory cytokines that began a cascade ending in multiorgan failure; the autopsy findings were read as initial lung injury followed by days of hypotension and ischaemia, and the authors call the significance of the cells' reactivity against cultured primary cells unclear. This is a single case, with a stated dose and conditioning, whose mechanism is the authors' hypothesis and which gives no incidence for any CAR product (Morgan et al., 2010). In a trial of an affinity-enhanced T-cell receptor against HLA-A*01-restricted MAGE-A3 in myeloma and melanoma, the first two patients developed cardiogenic shock and died within days; no MAGE-A3 expression was detected in heart tissue at autopsy, and beating cardiomyocytes made from induced pluripotent stem cells triggered T-cell killing through recognition of an unrelated peptide from titin. That is off-target recognition of an unintended molecule, not the intended target in the wrong tissue (Linette et al., 2013).

How the question is asked before and during trials. FDA's CAR T-cell development guidance says to assess both undesired targeting of healthy tissue that expresses the intended antigen (on-target/off-tumour) and unintended targeting of other antigens, using examples such as tissue cross-reactivity studies with an antibody carrying the same recognition domain, protein arrays, cytotoxicity and cytokine-release testing on panels of primary cells, cell lines or stem-cell-derived organ systems, and relevant animal models, and encourages a combination of methods; antigen recognition domains can differ in affinity or avidity or recognise a different site, which should be evaluated, and CAR T cells can carry added components such as suicide genes. In practice a readout is a staining intensity or positive fraction, a binding profile, killing or cytokine release by healthy cells at a named time, and finally organ injury in the treated population; stained fixed tissue does not show a living organ's accessibility, an animal model may lack the human target, and a negative result in one panel is not a safety certificate. No universal expression cut-off is given here because no source read gives one. Whether affinity tuning, recognition logic or control switches improve safety for a particular design needs that design's own evidence. The 2026 ASTCT consensus abstract lists on-target, off-tumour toxicity among the toxicities for which it considered definitions and grading; its criteria were not readable.

fields.after: Pulmonary function tests measure airflow, lung volume and gas transfer. They can describe a baseline or change in function, while clinical assessment identifies its cause.

A full set has three parts. Spirometry has the person breathe in fully and blow out as hard and as long as possible, measuring the forced vital capacity (FVC) and how fast air leaves; the forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) and its ratio to FVC are the usual numbers. The ATS/ERS 2019 spirometry standard describes the test as the maximal volume of air a person can inspire and expire with maximal effort, reports FEV1/FVC as a decimal fraction, and sets acceptability and repeatability criteria for each manoeuvre, so a poor-effort test is a quality problem before it is a finding. Spirometry is used to look for obstructive conditions, in which the airways narrow so air flows out with difficulty, as in asthma, bronchitis and emphysema (MedlinePlus). A lung volume test, often done by body plethysmography in a sealed booth, measures the total lung capacity (TLC), the amount of air the lungs can hold; restrictive conditions, in which the lungs cannot fill fully, such as pulmonary fibrosis and interstitial lung disease, lower it. The diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) has the person breathe in a gas mixture with a trace of carbon monoxide and a tracer gas, hold the breath for about 10 seconds and breathe out; it shows how well gas crosses into the blood. The ERS/ATS 2022 interpretation standard explains that a low DLCO with normal alveolar volume can be consistent with pulmonary vascular impairment, emphysema with preserved volume or anaemia. Low alveolar volume with low or normal transfer coefficient can accompany interstitial lung disease or emphysema with loss of lung volume. These are patterns to interpret, not diagnoses from one value. The 2017 ERS/ATS standard asks for no smoking or other carbon-monoxide exposure on the day of the test, recording the last cigarette and accounting for recent or heavy exposure. Its preparation instructions are technical test conditions, not an individual treatment plan.

How a result is judged. A value is compared with a healthy reference population for the person's age, sex and height. The ERS/ATS 2022 technical standard defines the lower limit of normal as the 5th percentile, a z-score of minus 1.645, so 5 per cent of a healthy reference population lie below that limit by definition. It strongly discourages the fixed cut-offs of 80 per cent of predicted for FEV1 and 0.70 for the FEV1/FVC ratio, because percent of predicted ignores how measurement variability changes with age, and it adds the qualifier that neither simple cut-offs nor the 5th percentile should be used as absolute diagnostic criteria, since healthy and diseased values overlap in a zone of uncertainty. Ideally the comparison is with the person's own earlier baseline. Serial results need their test quality, measurement variability and clinical context. A threshold developed for another test or population should not be turned into a universal DLCO monitoring rule. For DLCO the standard says the importance of haemoglobin cannot be overemphasised and all interpretations must have the reference values adjusted for haemoglobin, with particular care when people are monitored for drug toxicity and haemoglobin shifts, as in chemotherapy. A 2024 transplant cohort report likewise states that DLCO is affected by haemoglobin and that two adjustment equations (Cotes, recommended by ATS/ERS, and Dinakara) gave different results, so the method should be named.

Their place in drug-related lung injury. A baseline records a person's own starting point, which makes a later change easier to read than a comparison with a population average. In diagnosis the tests are one input: an Italian multidisciplinary expert-opinion panel on drug-induced interstitial lung disease lists spirometry and DLCO among the diagnostic components alongside history, vital signs including oxygen saturation, laboratory and microbial tests to exclude infection, and computed tomography, stratifies management by CTCAE grade, and notes that there were no specific guidelines at the time (Conte et al., 2022). In follow-up, repeat testing can show whether function is recovering or worsening. They do not replace imaging: the trastuzumab deruxtecan label asks for symptom monitoring and radiographic evaluation of suspected interstitial lung disease, and neither it nor the datopotamab deruxtecan label mentions scheduled breathing tests. For scale, adjudicated drug-related interstitial lung disease occurred in 12.1 per cent of patients given trastuzumab deruxtecan in DESTINY-Breast04, 0.8 per cent grade 5 (Modi et al., 2022), and a prior lung event can bear on eligibility for later treatment. A test pattern does not identify cause, since many conditions lower DLCO; that normal spirometry does not rule out interstitial disease is an evidence-reading distinction between airflow and gas transfer; the 2022 standard also states that a result within the reference range does not exclude disease.
