fields.after: A chemical probe is a compound used in the laboratory to switch one biological process off or on and ask what it does, so it is judged by how well it is characterised for that question and not by whether it could be given to a person.

A chemical probe is a research compound used to perturb a defined biological process in cells or animals. It is useful only to the extent that it is potent enough, selective enough and characterised well enough for the question being asked. Arrowsmith and colleagues put the requirement as a probe that is potent, of known selectivity and with a proven mechanism of action, and describe how many probes in common use were first characterised inadequately and later proved to be nonselective. LY294002 was described in 1994 as a selective inhibitor of PI3 kinase and was still sold as one by nearly all vendors, although by 2005 it was clear that it inhibited many other proteins at the concentrations used to inhibit PI3 kinase. An effect seen in cells at a high concentration therefore identifies an effect at that concentration, not necessarily a target.

The numerical standards belong to the groups that set them. For probes of epigenetic targets, the Structural Genomics Consortium as described by Arrowsmith and colleagues asks minimally for in vitro potency at the target below 100 nM, more than 30-fold selectivity over related proteins of the same family, profiling against a standard panel of off-targets and effects on the target in cells below 1 uM, and now requires an inactive close analogue as a negative control. Workman and Collins advocate assessing fitness for the intended experiment rather than applying an overly restrictive universal rule. Those cut-offs were written for particular target classes and do not apply to every probe, and neither paper offers a number that makes a concentration universally clean.

Controls carry the causal argument. An inactive or weakly active analogue from the same chemical family asks whether the effect follows the target-binding feature rather than shared chemistry; an active probe of a different chemical structure asks whether an independent perturbation agrees, with the limit that two probes can still share an off-target; and a genetic change or engineered resistance asks whether altering the target alters the effect as predicted, with the limit that removing a whole protein is different from blocking one of its functions. Workman and Collins add that a chemical probe can inhibit a specific function rather than remove the protein, which RNA interference cannot, and that both approaches have off-target as well as on-target effects. Agreement among these tests strengthens an inference, and conflicts should be recorded rather than set aside.

A probe is not a medicine. Arrowsmith and colleagues note that a probe does not need to meet the requirements of a successful medicine, such as good pharmacodynamics and oral bioavailability, and that high-quality probes have served as seeds for new medicines. A medicine also needs evidence in people about product quality, exposure, tolerability and benefit for its intended use, so a useful probe may lack adequate delivery, stability or safety, and an approved medicine can be a poor tool for isolating one target if several of its interactions contribute to its effects; this is an evidence-reading distinction rather than a claim that the same experiment establishes clinical suitability. A culture concentration is not a patient dose.

Target engagement is the separate question of whether a compound interacts with its target where the experiment needs it. The cellular thermal shift assay, introduced by Martinez Molina and colleagues, is built on ligand-induced thermal stabilisation of target proteins and was used to monitor drug binding in cells and tissue samples; a shift can support engagement under the assay conditions and is not by itself an inhibition or occupancy percentage. Engagement, a change in target function and cell survival are three measurements, and an effect on viability does not identify the responsible target.

Worked example, fictional. A new compound lowers the viability of cultured cells at 10 micromoles per litre, and neither engagement nor selectivity has been measured. The supported statement is that the compound has an effect in this culture at this concentration. It does not show that a particular protein is essential, and it does not show that a safe human dose reaches that protein. To close those gaps one would measure engagement and relevant selectivity, test an inactive analogue and a chemically different probe, and perturb the target genetically or by engineered resistance. Those steps address causality; exposure, quality, safety and clinical evidence remain separate questions.

fields.after: A drug target is the molecule or structure a treatment acts on and its mechanism of action is how that action produces an effect, and each step from target to patient benefit needs its own evidence.

A drug target is a biological molecule or structure that a treatment acts on, and the mechanism of action explains how that action produces an effect. The National Cancer Institute describes targeted therapy as treatment that targets proteins that control how cancer cells grow, divide and spread, and says most targeted therapies are small-molecule drugs, which are small enough to enter cells and so suit targets inside cells, or monoclonal antibodies, which are designed to attach to specific targets on cancer cells. It describes antibodies that mark cancer cells for the immune system, antibodies that stop growth or cause self-destruction directly, and antibodies that carry toxins to cancer cells. These are different jobs, so a shared label of targeted does not make the mechanisms interchangeable, and a target that is only an address for delivery need not drive the cancer's growth.

An altered gene or an elevated protein can suggest a target hypothesis; it does not show that inhibiting the target will harm cancer cells selectively, which controlled perturbations of the target test, and safe exposure and appropriate clinical studies answer later questions. Naming a target answers only the first of several questions. Binding is an interaction between molecules and can be shown with a purified protein, which does not show that the compound reaches the protein inside a cell. Target engagement asks whether the interaction occurs in the relevant cells or tissue, and exposure, target location and the cell membrane all bear on it; a blood concentration and a concentration at an intracellular target are different observations. The cellular thermal shift assay of Martinez Molina and colleagues was developed to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples, and its authors used it to monitor drug transport and activation, off-target effects and resistance in cancer cell lines. Binding is also different from changing function: a compound can inhibit an enzyme, activate a receptor or deliver a payload, and a binder can leave the target's activity unchanged. Binding assays test an interaction under specified conditions and engagement assays examine the relevant cells or tissue, while a downstream signal measures a biological consequence and is not automatically a direct measure of how much of the target is occupied; growth, death and regrowth assays add further layers. A measured change in signalling, division or survival needs controls that test the proposed explanation, and one positive experiment should not carry the whole claim.

The last step is clinical. Mechanistic plausibility does not show benefit, because the target may also be present in healthy tissue and the useful margin depends on achieved benefit and harm in a stated disease, treatment setting, product and outcome. The National Cancer Institute adds that cancer cells can become resistant to targeted therapy when the target itself changes so the drug can no longer interact with it, or when cells find new ways to grow that do not depend on the target.

Worked example, fictional. An antibody binds protein A on cancer cells, and a growth assay shows no change. Binding is supported under the assay conditions. It has not been shown that protein A drives growth, that the antibody inhibits protein A's function, that a finished payload-bearing product delivers anything, or that the product is safe and beneficial; each of those needs its own evidence. Before saying a drug worked, name the layer that was measured.

after: ovarian-function-after-chemotherapy

Temporary ovarian suppression during chemotherapy aims to reduce chemotherapy-induced ovarian insufficiency. It is a different use from ovarian suppression as endocrine treatment of hormone-receptor-positive cancer. Pulsatile hypothalamic gonadotropin-releasing hormone normally signals to the pituitary to release follicle-stimulating and luteinising hormones. The goserelin label describes a transient initial rise in oestrogen in women with breast cancer, followed by pituitary down-regulation with continued agonist exposure and suppression of ovarian hormone production. The 3.6 mg formulation uses a 28-day schedule in its label; this is a product description, not a schedule for every agonist or indication. It usually stops ovulation and menstruation during use, but does not ensure contraception. Hormone levels generally return after stopping, while chemotherapy-related ovarian injury can still prevent recovery. The classical Belchetz experiments compared continuous and intermittent GnRH delivery in rhesus monkeys; they established a pattern-dependent pituitary response rather than a breast-cancer treatment effect. The mechanism of ovarian protection during chemotherapy remains unsettled, so quieter ovaries do not guarantee preserved eggs or future pregnancy.

Keep each trial's endpoint, population and missing data visible. POEMS/SWOG S0230 randomised 257 premenopausal women with operable hormone-receptor-negative breast cancer. Among 135 with complete primary-endpoint data, ovarian failure at two years was 8% with goserelin and 22% without, odds ratio 0.30 (95% confidence interval 0.09 to 0.97); failure meant no menses in the preceding six months and postmenopausal FSH. Missing data weaken interpretation. The final analysis included 218 eligible and evaluable participants and reported five-year cumulative incidence of at least one pregnancy of 23.1% versus 12.2%. The disease-free-survival hazard ratio was 0.55 (95% confidence interval 0.27 to 1.10; P = 0.09). This secondary analysis did not establish a survival benefit, equivalence or an individual safety guarantee.

PROMISE-GIM6 randomised 281 premenopausal women with stage I to III breast cancer. Triptorelin began at least one week before chemotherapy and was given every four weeks for its duration in that trial. Early menopause, defined by absent menstrual recovery and postmenopausal FSH and oestradiol one year after chemotherapy, occurred in 8.9% versus 25.9%, odds ratio 0.28 (95% confidence interval 0.14 to 0.59). Lambertini and colleagues' individual-patient meta-analysis included 873 participants from five trials: premature ovarian insufficiency was 14.1% versus 30.9%, adjusted odds ratio 0.38 (95% confidence interval 0.26 to 0.57); at least one later pregnancy was reported by 10.3% versus 5.5%. The adjusted disease-free-survival hazard ratio was 1.01 (95% confidence interval 0.72 to 1.42). Those pooled results are not specific to triple-negative disease and do not prove absence of harm.

The 2025 ASCO fertility-preservation guideline says a GnRH agonist may be offered as an adjunct to females with breast cancer and should not replace established preservation methods such as egg, embryo or ovarian-tissue cryopreservation. The trials above compared chemotherapy with or without an agonist, not an agonist against freezing. Lower ovarian-failure rates therefore do not guarantee pregnancy. Menstrual suppression during treatment is not proof of permanent ovarian failure, and returning periods do not establish normal ovarian reserve or fertility. Early menopause also has consequences beyond fertility. NCI describes hot flushes, vaginal dryness and loss of libido, and longer-term bone loss and cardiovascular concerns with primary ovarian insufficiency. Reproductive assessment and the cancer-treatment indication are separate questions. Discussing preservation before cancer-directed treatment can preserve options; the guideline also addresses post-treatment preservation for people who did not undergo it earlier or stored insufficient material. Treatment-induced loss of ovarian function is not established by amenorrhoea during temporary suppression alone. The ovarian-failure proportions in these comparisons fell by roughly half or more relative to their comparison groups; that describes a named failure endpoint, not the probability of pregnancy or a comparison with freezing.

Chemotherapy can damage ovarian follicles containing immature eggs. NCI identifies alkylating agents as a high-risk group and describes risk as depending on age, baseline fertility, treatment type, dose and duration. Primary ovarian insufficiency can include intermittent ovulation or occasional periods; it should not be equated automatically with permanent sterility. Arecco and colleagues' 2021 review describes reduced recruitment of follicles and reduced ovarian perfusion as proposed explanations for protection by GnRH agonists, while noting that the mechanism is not fully clear. The clinical comparisons do not establish which mechanism caused the observed difference.

fields.before: Almost every lymphoma drug that finds the cancer by a surface marker finds healthy cells carrying the same marker. The side effects are not accidents; they are the treatment working on the wrong cells, and they are predictable from the marker.
fields.after: Some lymphoma treatments recognise lineage antigens shared with healthy cells. Those normal-cell targets can explain particular harms; cytokine-mediated effects and unintended binding are different mechanisms.

fields.before:
Nearly all the surface targets in lymphoma are what the corpus calls lineage antigens: normal proteins on a normal cell type, present on the cancer because the cancer came from that cell type. Only a few, such as CD30, are close to restricted to activated cells in an adult. This has consequences that can be read off the target before the first dose.

CD20 and CD19 are on every normal B cell, so anti-CD20 and anti-CD19 treatments empty the B-cell compartment. What follows is low immunoglobulin, more bacterial and viral infection, a blunted response to vaccination, and, specifically, reactivation of hepatitis B, which is why surface antigen and core antibody are checked before the first dose of rituximab. After CAR-T the aplasia is deeper and longer, sometimes years, and immunoglobulin replacement is part of the plan rather than a rescue.

CD52 is on B cells, T cells, monocytes and dendritic cells, so alemtuzumab produces the most profound lymphopenia of any antibody used in lymphoma, with CD4 counts that can stay low for a year, and with it cytomegalovirus reactivation, Pneumocystis pneumonia and fungal infection.

CCR4 is on regulatory T cells as well as on the tumour, so mogamulizumab removes the cells that hold autoimmunity in check: rash is common, and giving it shortly before an allogeneic transplant has been associated with severe graft-versus-host disease.

CD47 is on red cells, where its job is to tell a macrophage not to eat them, so blocking it causes anaemia by design; the dosing strategy that made the class usable is a low priming dose followed by higher maintenance doses.

CD38 produces a laboratory problem rather than a clinical one: anti-CD38 antibodies bind CD38 on red cells and make the indirect antiglobulin test positive, masking real alloantibodies, so the transfusion laboratory must be warned before a crossmatch.

CD3 is not on the tumour at all in B-cell disease: it is the handle a bispecific antibody uses to grip a T cell. Cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity are that mechanism working, which is why these drugs are given with step-up dosing.

drug-target-and-mechanism

Target, mechanism and evidence. A drug target is the molecule or structure a treatment acts on, and its mechanism of action is how that action produces an effect; a target name does not show that the target is reachable, required by the cancer, or that changing it does useful work. Binding to a purified protein, engagement in the relevant cell (the cellular thermal shift assay was introduced to evaluate drug binding in cells and tissues), a measured effect with controls, and benefit and harm in a stated clinical setting each need their own evidence, and a blood concentration is not the concentration at an intracellular target. In-cell thermal profiling can pick up indirect as well as direct targets (Ball et al. 2020). If an antibody is shown to bind a protein on cancer cells and growth is unchanged, binding is supported; dependence on the protein, inhibition of its function, delivery by a finished payload-bearing product, safety and benefit are not. A molecule used as an address for delivery and a molecule whose function the cell depends on are different roles.

What NCI says about the class. Targeted therapy was once expected to be less toxic than chemotherapy but can cause serious side effects, cancer cells can become resistant to it, and it may work best combined with other targeted therapy or with treatments such as chemotherapy and radiation (NCI page, HTML read).

after: Dose, dosage, cumulative dose and dose intensity are different quantities. Dose is the quantity of drug (state the drug, the formulation and whether it is per administration or per day; milligrams, milligrams per kilogram and milligrams per square metre are different scales), and dosage is the dose with its schedule, meaning the interval between doses and the duration of treatment (FDA, 'Optimizing the Dosage of Human Prescription Drugs and Biological Products for the Treatment of Oncologic Diseases', August 2024, which says it does not specifically address several modalities). Cumulative dose adds the amounts given over a course. Dose intensity is the amount of a named drug delivered per unit time, commonly milligrams per square metre per week, and relative dose intensity divides delivered by a stated reference intensity, so it needs the reference regimen and method named; a delay lowers delivered intensity in the same proportion as an equal dose reduction, and the link between delivered intensity and response or survival has not been fully demonstrated (Alberto 1995). Equal milligrams of different medicines are not equivalent activity, and a body-size-normalised dose is not a laboratory concentration. Teaching arithmetic with invented units, not data: four 10-unit administrations over a 4-week window give 40 units and 10 units per week; the same four over 8 weeks give 5 units per week, 50 per cent of the first intensity, which says nothing about benefit, exposure or safety.

A fictional reference intensity of 10 arbitrary units per week and delivered intensity of 8 gives relative dose intensity 8/10 = 0.8, or 80%. Neither that ratio nor a body-size-normalised administered dose measures the concentration at a target or the probability of benefit. For combinations, declare how the individual drugs' normalised ratios are summarised rather than adding milligrams of different substances.

Class effects versus product figures. US labels report brentuximab vedotin peripheral neuropathy of any grade in 62 per cent of patients in monotherapy studies; mirvetuximab soravtansine ocular adverse reactions in 59 per cent of patients with ovarian cancer, grade 3 in 11 per cent; belantamab mafodotin dosage modification for ocular toxicity in 83 per cent of patients in its clinical study, with a boxed warning and a restricted programme; and tisotumab vedotin a boxed warning for severe ocular toxicity, including severe vision loss and corneal ulceration, with an ophthalmic examination before every cycle for the first nine. Datopotamab deruxtecan: stomatitis in 63 per cent and ocular adverse reactions in 38 per cent of 1,365 patients treated as a single agent at 6 mg/kg in the pooled label population. Trastuzumab emtansine carries a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity, cardiac toxicity and embryo-fetal toxicity. The sacituzumab govitecan, trastuzumab deruxtecan and trastuzumab emtansine rates, and the datopotamab deruxtecan lung-disease rates, are in the record on ADC side effects in breast cancer. The figures come from different trials and populations and cannot be compared head to head, and sharing a payload class does not make products equivalent.

before: Dose intensity includes time. In a fictional single-drug course, a reference of 600 mg/m² over six weeks is 100 mg/m²/week. Giving 600 mg/m² over eight weeks gives 75 mg/m²/week, or 75% relative dose intensity; giving 450 mg/m² over six weeks produces the same ratio by a different change. These calculations assume the same body-surface-area basis and defined treatment interval. For combinations, report each drug's reference and how its ratio contributes to the combined measure. Alberto's 1995 overview describes average relative dose intensity as the mean of the component ratios, not a measure that by itself establishes an outcome.

Zhang et al. (2018) studied women diagnosed in Louisiana in 2011 with stage I to III breast cancer: 494 had hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative disease and 180 had triple-negative disease. Across five predefined cutoffs, their abstract reports that relative dose intensity below 85% was associated with worse overall survival in the hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative group (hazard ratio 1.93, 95% confidence interval 1.09 to 3.40). fields.before: When engineered T cells or a bispecific antibody switch on, the immune system can overshoot. The first sign is a fever, and the treatment is a drug that blocks the main signal, given early. A smaller number of people become confused or drowsy, which is graded and treated separately.
fields.after: Inflammatory and neurologic toxicities after immune-effector therapy need separate clinical assessment, grading and recovery records; the treatment plan depends on the product and findings.

fields.before:
The 2019 ASTCT consensus grades cytokine release syndrome by fever, hypotension and oxygen support. Fever is at least 38°C and not attributable to another cause. Grade 1 has no hypotension or hypoxia. Grade 2 adds hypotension not requiring vasopressors and/or low-flow nasal oxygen (up to 6 litres/minute) or blow-by. Grade 3 requires one vasopressor with or without vasopressin, and/or high-flow nasal oxygen or a face mask. Grade 4 requires multiple vasopressors excluding vasopressin, and/or positive-pressure ventilation. The more severe blood-pressure or oxygen-support criterion determines the grade; other causes must be excluded. In patients with CRS who then receive antipyretics or anti-cytokine treatment such as tocilizumab or steroids, fever is no longer required to grade subsequent CRS severity. Management escalates with grade: paracetamol and fluids; tocilizumab, an IL-6 receptor antibody, for grade 2 and above or for persistent grade 1; corticosteroids added for grade 3 and 4 or when tocilizumab does not work; intensive care for grade 4. Tocilizumab is given early rather than held back, because early use does not appear to reduce CAR-T efficacy.

ICANS, immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, is graded on the ICE score (orientation, naming, following commands, writing, attention), level of consciousness, seizures, motor findings and raised intracranial pressure or cerebral oedema. Handwriting deteriorates before anything else in many patients, which is why a daily written sentence is part of the observation chart. Corticosteroids, usually dexamethasone, are the treatment; tocilizumab does not cross into the brain and does not help ICANS alone. Seizure prophylaxis with levetiracetam is used with the products that carry the highest risk.

The risk differs by product and disease. Grade 3 or worse cytokine release syndrome was 13 per cent in ZUMA-1 and grade 3 or higher neurological events 28 per cent; in TRANSFORM with lisocabtagene maraleucel, grade 3 cytokine release syndrome was 1 per cent and grade 3 neurological events 4 per cent. Bispecific antibodies with step-up dosing sit lower again: 1.7 per cent grade 3 or worse cytokine release syndrome in the follicular cohort of ELM-2.

Late immune effector cell toxicities are now recognised too: prolonged cytopenias, a haemophagocytic picture, and an increased risk of infection for months.
fields.after:

Its grade follows the more severe attributable hypotension or hypoxia criterion. Grade 1 has neither; grade 2 includes hypotension not requiring vasopressors or low-flow nasal oxygen or blow-by. Grade 3 includes one vasopressor with or without vasopressin, or high-flow nasal oxygen or a face mask. Grade 4 includes multiple vasopressors excluding vasopressin, or positive-pressure support. Once an individual with CRS receives fever-reducing or anti-cytokine treatment, fever is no longer needed to grade subsequent severity.

ICANS assessment is separate. In the adult 2019 framework, the ICE cognitive screen is combined with consciousness, seizures, motor findings and signs of raised intracranial pressure or cerebral oedema, excluding other causes. Improvement of blood pressure or oxygenation does not establish neurologic recovery.

The scale reports severity; it does not determine a universal treatment algorithm, preventive medicine or order of symptom onset. Management follows the clinical findings, product guidance and care team's protocol. Trial toxicity rates require their own grading version, population, denominator and follow-up. The 2026 consensus expands the toxicity framework, but its detailed criteria were not accessible for this entry, so the numerical criteria here are explicitly historical 2019 criteria.

after: Target engagement and the evidence ladder. Target engagement asks whether a compound interacts with its intended target in the relevant system. Binding to a purified protein does not show that the compound enters the cell or reaches its target in a tumour, and engagement is also not a change in the target's function, a downstream effect or clinical benefit. Each question needs its own measurement: engagement first, then a measured biological effect, then a check of the causal explanation with controls, then clinical evidence.

Reading a thermal-shift result. The cellular thermal shift assay was introduced to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples through ligand-induced thermal stabilisation (Martinez Molina et al. 2013). The readout is the soluble target signal remaining after heating, plotted either against temperature at a fixed compound concentration or against concentration at a fixed temperature, so degrees Celsius and concentration units sit on different axes and the two designs ask different bounded questions. A shift of the compound curve against a matched control supports engagement under those conditions; indirect stability or protein-complex effects can also change the signal, so it is not an inhibition or occupancy percentage, and no universal shift cut-off is given here. The heated aliquots are consumed, so a record should carry the compound, concentration, exposure time, temperature series, cell or tissue system and controls. In an isothermal-shift study with a pan-kinase inhibitor, a large share of non-kinase proteins shifted in cells, which the authors read as in-cell profiling being more likely than lysate profiling to identify indirect binding targets; they recommend lysate profiling to identify targets and in-cell profiling to verify intracellular engagement (Ball et al. 2020).

Probes and medicines. Chemical probes are judged by potency, known selectivity and proven mechanism for the question asked, and the numerical criteria published for them belong to a consortium and target class (Arrowsmith et al. 2015; Workman and Collins 2010); a probe is a research starting point and not evidence of a usable medicine.

Record the named target and its detectability, baseline thermal behaviour, compound exposure, sample system and controls. In a temperature series, temperature changes while concentration is held fixed; in a concentration series, the selected temperature stays fixed. The output is soluble target signal, with different x-axis units in those two designs. Heated aliquots are consumed. An indirect stability change or protein-complex effect can alter the result, and neither a universal shift threshold nor a direct occupancy percentage follows from the plot.

after: Controls and their limits. In chemical-probe practice an inactive close analogue serves as a negative control and a second, structurally unrelated probe reduces the chance of shared off-targets (Arrowsmith et al. 2015). Genetic perturbation is a separate line of evidence, with its own limit: removing a whole protein can differ from inhibiting one of its functions (the teaching lesson's reasoning, not a result read). The nearest real example is natural reversion: ovarian cancer lines from one BRCA2 mutation carrier acquired a secondary BRCA2 mutation that restored BRCA2 and went with resistance to cisplatin and a PARP inhibitor, and transient siRNA depletion of BRCA2 re-sensitised the restored clones (Sakai et al. 2009); that is natural reversion plus knockdown in one patient's lineage, and depletion is not pharmacological inhibition. Agreement among controls supports a mechanism in the tested system only.

What to do next with a viability result. If a compound lowers viability in culture at one concentration, measure engagement and relevant selectivity, compare an inactive analogue and an independent probe, and use a suitable genetic perturbation or rescue; exposure, product quality, safety and clinical evidence remain separate questions that controls do not settle.

Class effects versus product figures. US labels report brentuximab vedotin peripheral neuropathy of any grade in 62 per cent of patients in monotherapy studies; mirvetuximab soravtansine ocular adverse reactions in 59 per cent of patients with ovarian cancer, grade 3 in 11 per cent; belantamab mafodotin dosage modification for ocular toxicity in 83 per cent of patients in its clinical study, with a boxed warning and a restricted programme; and tisotumab vedotin a boxed warning for severe ocular toxicity, including severe vision loss and corneal ulceration, with an ophthalmic examination before every cycle for the first nine. Datopotamab deruxtecan: stomatitis in 63 per cent and ocular adverse reactions in 38 per cent of 1,365 patients treated as a single agent at 6 mg/kg in the pooled label population. Trastuzumab emtansine carries a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity, cardiac toxicity and embryo-fetal toxicity. The sacituzumab govitecan, trastuzumab deruxtecan and trastuzumab emtansine rates, and the datopotamab deruxtecan lung-disease rates, are in the record on ADC side effects in breast cancer. The figures come from different trials and populations and cannot be compared head to head, and sharing a payload class does not make products equivalent.
